questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of substernal chest pain. He described it as burning and associated with swallowing solids and liquids. He had not had any vomiting, diarrhea, or blood in his stools. He was known to have HIV and intermittently took his antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis treatments. On oral examination there were white mucosal plaque lesions that easily scraped off but no ulcerations. Investigations: CD4 count 65 cells/μ L HIV-1 RNA viral load 22,150 copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Fluconazole The patient’s presentation with clinical symptoms suggestive of esophagitis and oral candidiasis (thrush) is most consistent with candida esophagitis, which is treated with fluconazole. Nystatin would be inadequate for esophageal involvement. Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus can also cause esophagitis but would be less common, particularly given the concomitant thrush. Pantoprazole, used for reflux esophagitis, would be a diagnosis of exclusion after infectious causes were ruled out.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q37

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man was reviewed with a 4-day history of fevers and hypotension despite empiric use of broadspectrum antibiotics. The man had presented to hospital 3 weeks earlier with profuse diarrhea and severe malnutrition. He had Crohn’s disease with short gut syndrome secondary to multiple bowel resections. He was initiated at admission on total parenteral nutrition via central venous catheter. His antimicrobials were changed to meropenem and micafungin. Investigations: Total white cell count 20 ×109/L Platelet count 50 ×109/L Blood cultures (central and peripheral) no growth after 3 days CXR: bilateral airspace disease
questions.lead_in: What is the best next test to secure a diagnosis?

options.text: Blood culture inoculated onto Sabouraud dextrose agar
Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil

questions.explanation: Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil This is a case of disseminated Malassezia infection. Risk factors in this case include CVC and lipid infusions (TPN). Malassezia spp. are intrinsically resistant to echinocandins, thus a response to micafungin is not expected. Malassezia spp. are lipophilic, and all species but M. pachydermatis require exogenous lipids for growth. M. furfur is the most common pathogen involved in disseminated disease. Recovery from standard blood cultures is low unless the media is enriched with fatty acids, i.e., with olive oil, palmitic acid, Tween, etc., or with Dixon’s agar, which contains glycerol mono-oleate. Serum 1,3- β-D-glucan is a nonspecific biomarker of fungal disease. It is not particularly helpful in making a diagnosis. Panfungal PCR is not useful on blood because of the low burden of organisms in the total circulation. Serum CrAg is used for the diagnosis of cryptococcosis (including subclinical disease). It also can cross react with Trichosporon spp. in disseminated disease, although a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. Trichosporonosis has been reported in neonates but is less likely than Malassezia disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q26

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presented for routine clinic review. She had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and was 4 years postrenal transplant. She denied urinary frequency, dysuria, or focal symptoms. Her graft function was excellent. Investigations: Urine microscopy: 30 leucocytes per high-powered field Urine culture: pure heavy growth of Candida species
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Reassurance only There is no indication to treat asymptomatic candiduria in this clinical context. Pyuria is not an indication for treatment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q21

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with a 5-week history of throat pain and difficulty swallowing. The odynophagia had worsened over time, limiting oral intake. He had had a negative rapid strep test and a 2-week course of penicillin without symptomatic response. He had 1 week of night sweats but no fever or chills. He had a dry cough for 2 weeks but no dyspnea. He had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and had renal transplantation 18 months prior. He had been born and brought up in Indonesia and had come to the United States for college. He had been screened for TB 4 years earlier and had had a chest X-ray then which showed a small linear opacity in the right lower lobe. Tuberculosis skin and sputum testing at that time was negative. Current medications included prednisone 7.5 mg daily, mycophenolate 1 gram twice daily, and tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily. On examination his temperature was 98.2°F. Tonsils and posterior pharynx were inflamed and erythematous. There were no exudates or other lesions. There were no other abnormalities on exam. Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe density with calcification, unchanged from previous films HIV antibody, CMV viral load, and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis were negative CT scan of the neck: thickening of the epiglottis and left piriform sinus On endoscopy, the true vocal cords were normal in appearance. The epiglottis was thickened and the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis and supraglottic folds had irregular white friable tissue.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis The patient presents with a chronic epiglottitis, on a background of immunocompromise due to immunosuppression for renal transplantation. Granulomatous diseases and malignancy must be considered in the differential diagnosis. Due to the patient’s history of being born in Indonesia, along with the radiographic abnormalities, tuberculosis is the likely diagnosis in this case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q6

questions.stem: A 35-year-old developed fungemia with Candida parapsilosis during a prolonged hospital course in the ICU with nonischemic heart failure. Her central lines were removed, surveillance cultures were negative, and echocardiogram was unrevealing. She was treated initially with caspofungin followed by fluconazole once speciation and sensitivities returned. Two weeks later, she lost vision in her right eye. Dilated eye exam revealed fluffy vitreal lesions. She had an urgent vitrectomy with intravitreal antifungal injection.
questions.lead_in: What systemic agent would be preferred for treatment?
questions.explanation: Voriconazole Voriconazole or fluconazole would be the best option as they penetrate the eye well, unless there are concerns for resistance. Her case is describing the natural course of endophthalmitis rather than treatment failure, and C. parapsilosis should be azole-sensitive. While amphotericin will penetrate the eye, she could avoid the toxicity by using an azole. The echinocandins have very poor penetration into the eye.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q10

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man was diagnosed with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) after recurrent infections from the age of 5 years old. Hypoparathyroidism was diagnosed after an episode of tetanic spasms at 10 years old. At 15 years of age, he developed adrenal insufficiency.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-17 axis

questions.explanation: APECED syndrome Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy–Candidiasis–Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED) or autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is characterized by the triad of CMC, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease. CARD9 deficiency and IL-17 deficiencies can also present with CMC but lack the endocrinopathies. Patients with MCM4 deficiency, on the other hand, also present with adrenal insufficiency, while patients with DiGeorge syndrome also have hypoparathyroidism.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q26

questions.model_answer:
a) Catheter: remove (or at least change) the central venous catheter — removal is almost always required for cure of catheter-associated candidemia. Antimicrobial: start empiric echinocandin (caspofungin 70 mg load then 50 mg IV daily, OR micafungin 100 mg IV daily, OR anidulafungin 200 mg load then 100 mg IV daily); also do funduscopic/ophthalmologic exam and repeat blood cultures.
b) Germ tube test — C. albicans is germ tube positive (forms true germ tubes; C. dubliniensis also positive).
c) No fundamental change — an echinocandin is the recommended first-line agent for candidemia including non-albicans species (C. glabrata, C. krusei). Continue the echinocandin; step down to fluconazole only if the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible, the patient is clinically stable and blood cultures have cleared.
d) Suspect Candida auris (frequently misidentified as C. haemulonii). Precautions: single room with contact precautions, notify infection prevention and public health/reference lab for confirmatory identification, and reinforce environmental disinfection and hand hygiene.
questions.beyond_mandell: C. auris misidentification as C. haemulonii and its infection-control measures (contact precautions, single room, public health notification) are CDC guidance, not in this chapter.

questions.model_answer:
a) MALDI-TOF MS with an updated/validated reference database, or molecular identification by rDNA sequencing (D1-D2 of 28S, or ITS). Conventional biochemical panels misidentify it.
b) Any two of: Candida haemulonii, Candida duobushaemulonii, Candida famata, Candida sake, or Saccharomyces species.
c) Remove the central venous catheter; start an echinocandin first-line (micafungin 100 mg IV daily, OR caspofungin 70 mg load then 50 mg daily, OR anidulafungin 200 mg load then 100 mg daily). Switch to liposomal amphotericin B 3-5 mg/kg/day if persistent fungemia or clinical non-response. Place on contact precautions and notify public health.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reliable C. auris identification methods and look-alike species are CDC guidance; the chapter only notes triazole activity is diminished against C. auris.

cohort_answer.text: Identification: PCR (D1-D2 or ITS sequencing of 28s rDNA) or MALDI-TOF. Similar species: C. haemulonii; also C. famata, C. sake, Rhodotorula glutinis, Rhodotorula mucilaginosa, Saccharomyces species; rarely C. catenulata, C. lusitaniae, C. guilliermondii, C. parapsilosis. Treatment: Remove line; initial caspofungin (load 70mg IV then 50mg IV daily) or micafungin 100mg IV daily; switch to liposomal ampho B 5mg/kg/day if clinically unresponsive or persistent fungemia >5 days (90% resistance to fluc, 30% to ampho, 5% echinocandins)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Blood cultures (candidemia/dissemination). (2) Lumbar puncture — CNS involvement is more frequent in neonates with candidemia, and LP should be considered whenever an infant's blood cultures grow Candida. (3) Dilated funduscopic/retinal examination for ocular candidiasis (plus consider renal/abdominal ultrasound).
b) Amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg IV daily.
c) It is well tolerated with low nephrotoxicity in neonates, achieves good CNS and urinary-tract penetration (neonates are at high risk of CNS dissemination), whereas echinocandins penetrate CNS/urine poorly with limited neonatal data, and fluconazole is less favoured here.

questions.model_answer:
a) Transesophageal echocardiography.
b) (1) Liposomal amphotericin B 3-5 mg/kg IV daily, with or without flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO q6h. (2) High-dose echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin 150 mg IV daily or micafungin 150 mg IV daily) as an alternative parenteral induction regimen. Either is a bridge to valve replacement, followed by 6-8 weeks of therapy after surgery and long-term/lifelong oral azole suppression.
c) (1) Addiction medicine consultation with opioid agonist therapy and harm reduction (naloxone, sterile injecting supplies, safe injection education). (2) Dilated ophthalmologic examination to exclude Candida endophthalmitis, and commitment to long-term/lifelong oral azole suppression after induction therapy.
d) (1) Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction (severe regurgitation, perforation, dehiscence). (2) Perivalvular abscess, fistula, or new heart block. (3) Persistent bacteremia or fever beyond 5-7 days on appropriate antimicrobial therapy. (4) Recurrent embolism with a persistent or enlarging vegetation, or vegetation >10 mm with severe valvular regurgitation. (5) Prosthetic valve endocarditis, or infection with an organism unlikely to be cured medically (Staphylococcus aureus PVE, multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacilli).
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA candidiasis 2016 and AHA 2015: high-dose echinocandin is an accepted alternative to lipid amphotericin B with or without flucytosine, with chronic fluconazole suppression; Mandell's text names amphotericin B products as initial therapy.

questions.model_answer:
a) C. haemulonii is commonly a misidentified Candida auris — an emerging, often multidrug-resistant pathogen that transmits in healthcare settings, so this is both a resistance and an infection-control concern.
b) Approximate CDC US figures: fluconazole ~90%, amphotericin B ~30%, echinocandins ~5% (echinocandin is the best empiric choice pending susceptibilities).
c) (1) Place the patient in a single room on contact precautions. (2) Notify infection prevention and local public health/CDC, and send for confirmatory identification. (3) Enforce environmental cleaning/disinfection (e.g., bleach or EPA-approved sporicidal) and hand hygiene; screen epidemiologically linked contacts.

questions.model_answer:
a) Germ tube test.
b) The yeast is incubated in serum at 37°C for ~2-3 hours; C. albicans forms true germ tubes (filamentous outgrowths without constriction at their base) = positive. Other Candida species are negative. Note C. dubliniensis is also germ tube positive (it can be separated by lack of growth at 45°C).
questions.beyond_mandell: Methodologic details (serum, 37°C ~3 h, C. dubliniensis also positive, 45°C distinction) are general mycology, beyond this chapter which only states the germ tube test identifies C. albicans.

cohort_answer.text: Test: Germ tube test. Interpretation: Screening test to differentiate Candida albicans from other yeast; grown in human/sheep serum at 37°C for 3 hours, forms germ tube detected via wet KOH films as filamentous outgrowth; positive for Candida albicans and Candida dubliniensis. Minimum 5 germ tubes should be observed before calling positive. Growth at 45°C separates C. albicans from C. dubliniensis.

questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA candidiasis 2016 and AHA 2015: high-dose echinocandin is an accepted alternative to lipid amphotericin B with or without flucytosine, with chronic fluconazole suppression; Mandell's text names amphotericin B products as initial therapy.

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: Liposomal Amphotericin B 3-5mg/kg IV daily +/- flucytosine 25mg/kg PO QID; Micafungin 150mg IV daily followed by lifelong suppression (fluconazole monotherapy for initial therapy has higher failure). Other interventions: TEE (abscess), ophthalmologic exam. Surgery indications: persistent blood culture positivity (≥7 days), vegetation ≥1cm with evidence of embolization, symptomatic heart failure, abscess, prosthetic valve.

What are 4 indications for early surgery other than fungal infection?

questions.model_answer:
a) Echocardiography, preferably transesophageal (TEE) — to assess for Candida endocarditis; TEE improves sensitivity, particularly for the mitral valve.
b) (1) Liposomal amphotericin B, with or without flucytosine. (2) A high-dose echinocandin (e.g., micafungin 150 mg daily). Give ≥6 weeks (longer with complications) with step-down/long-term fluconazole suppression if susceptible.
c) Early valve replacement surgery (strongly recommended, do not delay) and removal of intravascular catheters, with repeat blood cultures, funduscopic exam and long-term fluconazole suppression.
d) From infective-endocarditis surgical criteria: (1) heart failure from valve dysfunction; (2) uncontrolled infection — perivalvular abscess, heart block, or persistent bacteremia despite therapy; (3) prevention of embolism — large/mobile vegetation >10 mm, especially after an embolic event; (4) prosthetic valve dehiscence/instability.
questions.beyond_mandell: The four non-fungal surgical indications are from AHA/ESC infective-endocarditis guidelines; the chapter does not enumerate them.

cohort_answer.text: TEE. First line therapies: L-AMB with or without flucytosine, or echinocandin (increased dose e.g. micafungin 150mg) for at least 6-10 weeks after surgery; can switch to fluconazole if susceptible Candida + clinically stable + cleared BCx; valve replacement/surgery should not wait; close monitoring and often fluconazole as long-term suppressive therapy. (For candidal endocarditis: AmpB+flucytosine has mortality benefit vs monotherapy, fungicidal, step down to PO fluconazole if susceptible; for candidemia, echinocandins or fluconazole appropriate first-line per IDSA 2016; lifelong suppression fluconazole 400-800mg daily if NVIE/PVIE without valve surgery.) Interventions: Early valve replacement surgery for fungal endocarditis (mortality benefit); at least 6 weeks of therapy (longer if abscess/complications), followed by lifelong azole therapy regardless of surgical status (AHA/IDSA 2015 IE guidelines - reasonable in patients post valve surgery; Candida guidelines differ, suggesting suppression only if not surgical candidate or prosthetic valve). (4 indications for early surgery other than fungal infection: not documented in source.)

questions.model_answer:
a) The real concern is misidentified Candida auris. C. haemulonii is a common misidentification of C. auris by older biochemical/automated platforms, and C. auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant yeast that is highly transmissible in healthcare settings and causes invasive disease with high mortality. New York is a recognized U.S. endemic focus. It matters because it drives both antifungal choice and aggressive infection-control action.
b) Approximate resistance: fluconazole >90%; amphotericin B ~15-30%; echinocandins ~2-10% (echinocandins are the preferred empiric agent).
c) (1) Notify the microbiology lab to confirm identification with MALDI-TOF/molecular methods and notify public health. (2) Notify infection prevention and control, place the patient in a single room on contact precautions with dedicated equipment and enhanced/terminal cleaning. (3) Screen close contacts/co-located patients (axilla and groin swabs) for colonization and reinforce hand hygiene.
questions.beyond_mandell: Resistance percentages and the C. auris identification/infection-control bundle are from CDC/PHAC C. auris guidance; this Mandell slice notes only that triazoles have diminished activity against C. auris and lists it as an emerging multidrug-resistant species.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Liposomal amphotericin B (polyene); (2) an echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin or micafungin). b) (1) Acute heart failure from severe aortic regurgitation (valvular dysfunction); (2) fungal IE — ineffective/inadequate antimicrobial therapy for an organism that cannot be eradicated medically; (3) large vegetation >1 cm (1.2 cm). c) Suppressive antifungal therapy after an initial induction course: long-term (often lifelong) oral fluconazole suppression for patients who cannot undergo valve replacement.

questions.question: Candida albicans identification.
questions.question_raw: Candida albicans.

parts.text: What is the rapid test for it?
How do you interpret the test?

parts_raw.text: What is the rapid test for it
How to interpret test?

questions.model_answer:
a) The germ tube test.
b) The yeast is suspended in serum and incubated ~2-3 hours at 35-37 degrees C; a positive test is the appearance of short, non-septate, non-constricted filamentous outgrowths (germ tubes) arising directly from the yeast cell without a constriction at the point of origin. A positive germ tube test gives a rapid presumptive identification of C. albicans (C. dubliniensis also gives a positive result); a negative result points to a non-albicans species, and definitive speciation then relies on other physiologic/molecular methods (e.g., MALDI-TOF MS).

cohort_answer.text: Germ tube test. A rapid presumptive identification of C. albicans can be made by placing organism in serum and observing germ tube formation (small projections appearing within 90 min); used to differentiate C. albicans (and C. dubliniensis) from other Candida spp. Interpretation: sample placed in tube with sheep serum, incubated 2-4h, drop placed on slide with KOH prep - see filamentous outgrowth extending from yeast cells; positive germ tube test = C. albicans (or C. dubliniensis), based on non-constricted germ tube arising from yeast; false-negative and false-positive germ tube formations may occur; remainder of speciation relies on physiologic parameters rather than morphology.

questions.question: A man has repeat positive urine cultures for Candida and pyuria. He has a known stone but no obstruction.

parts.text: Would you treat?
If so, with what?

parts_raw.text: Would you treat
If so, with what?

questions.model_answer:
a) No. Asymptomatic candiduria usually resolves without antifungal therapy and treatment is not indicated. Treatment is reserved for symptomatic patients or those at high risk for dissemination: neutropenic patients, very-low-birth-weight infants, renal transplant recipients, and patients undergoing urologic instrumentation or with urinary tract obstruction. A stone without obstruction and no dissemination risk does not warrant treatment; treat instead if he is symptomatic or about to undergo an instrumentation/urologic procedure.
b) If treatment is indicated (e.g., symptomatic cystitis or planned instrumentation), oral fluconazole 200 mg (3 mg/kg) daily for ~2 weeks for a susceptible isolate; alternatives are AMB-D 0.3-0.6 mg/kg for 1-7 days or flucytosine. Relief of any obstruction and removal of stents/catheters is the primary step. Fungus balls require surgical removal.
c) The germ tube test.

cohort_answer.text: No treatment for asymptomatic candiduria unless high risk for dissemination (neutropenic patients, very low-birth-weight infants <1500g, patients undergoing urologic manipulation); renal transplantation no longer an absolute indication, consider case-by-case (UpToDate). Treatment: not recommended unless high-risk group; neutropenic/VLBW infants treated as for candidemia; patients undergoing urologic procedures: oral fluconazole 400mg (6mg/kg) daily OR AmB deoxycholate 0.3-0.6mg/kg daily for several days before/after procedure; for symptomatic cystitis: oral fluconazole 200mg (3mg/kg) daily x2 weeks, alternatively 1-7 days amphoB deoxycholate or flucytosine x7-10 days; if treating pyelo with amphoB can add flucytosine; do not use lipid formulations of amphoB (does not concentrate in kidney/bladder). Distinguishing test: Germ tube testing.

parts.text: What initial empiric antifungal therapy (from two different classes) would you use?
State three indications for urgent surgery present in this case.

parts_raw.text: What initial empiric antifungal therapy (from 2 different classes) would you use?
What are 3 indications for urgent surgery present in this case.
He is deemed not a candidate for valvular surgery. Based on the 2016 AHA/IDSA guidelines, what is the recommended antifungal management in this case?

questions.model_answer:
a) Initial empiric antifungal therapy combining two classes: (1) a polyene — lipid/liposomal amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg/day), preferably with flucytosine (25 mg/kg/dose QID); PLUS (2) a high-dose echinocandin. Mandell notes amphotericin B plus 5-fluorocytosine and that echinocandins are encouraging for fungal IE.
b) Three indications for urgent surgery present here: (1) Fungal (Candida) endocarditis — infection that cannot be eradicated with antimicrobial therapy alone (ineffective antimicrobial therapy); (2) Severe aortic regurgitation with heart failure (hemodynamic compromise/CHF), the crucial determinant for valve replacement; (3) Large vegetation (13 mm) with systemic embolic phenomena (multiple splenic lesions).
c) When not a surgical candidate: complete the induction course with amphotericin B-based therapy and document clearance of candidemia, then step down (if the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible and the patient is stable) to oral fluconazole 400-800 mg (6-12 mg/kg) daily as long-term/lifelong chronic suppressive therapy because of the high risk of relapse.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific step-down-to-fluconazole and lifelong suppression strategy is from the 2016 AHA IE scientific statement / IDSA Candida guidelines; Mandell confirms only long-term suppressive antifungal therapy in general.

cohort_answer.text: Empiric therapy: Liposomal amphoB (3-5mg/kg) +/- flucytosine; High dose echinocandin. Urgent surgery indications: Fungal endocarditis; Severe heart failure with valve dysfunction; Large mobile vegetation with evidence of embolic phenomena. If not a surgical candidate: Step down therapy to fluconazole 400-800mg daily if susceptible isolates, clinical stability, and cleared bloodstream Candida; for patients who cannot undergo valve replacement, long term suppression with fluconazole 400-800mg daily if isolate susceptible; even with surgery, reasonable to consider lifelong prophylaxis due to recurrence risk

questions.question: A patient is 30 days out from an allogeneic transplant complicated by severe Candida mucositis treated with fluconazole, and now has increasing liver enzymes.
questions.question_raw: A patient is 30 days out from an allogeneic transplant which was complicated by severe candida mucositis and treated with fluconazole. Now has increasing LFTs.

parts.text: What is the probable cause?
What would you do with this patient now? Justify your answer.

parts_raw.text: What is the probable cause?
What would you do with this patient now? Justify your answer

questions.model_answer:
a) The most probable cause is fluconazole (azole) hepatotoxicity. The key differential is hepatosplenic (chronic disseminated) candidiasis, which classically becomes manifest during recovery from neutropenia around engraftment; other considerations include sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/VOD, acute GVHD, viral hepatitis (CMV, HSV, HHV6, hepatitis viruses), and other hepatotoxic drugs (calcineurin inhibitors, methotrexate, TMP-SMX).
b) (1) Investigate: check LFT pattern and trend, and obtain cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI/US of liver and spleen) looking for the characteristic small abscesses of hepatosplenic candidiasis, plus blood cultures for yeast. (2) Stop the fluconazole given the transaminitis and switch antifungal cover to an echinocandin (or a lipid-formulation amphotericin B), which are the recommended agents for chronic disseminated/hepatosplenic candidiasis and avoid ongoing azole hepatotoxicity; if an azole is later required, posaconazole is better tolerated. (3) Exclude the competing diagnoses (viral serologies/PCR, review of hepatotoxic drugs, assess for VOD/GVHD). Justification: fever and abnormal LFTs long after culture-negativity are typical of hepatosplenic candidiasis, which requires prolonged echinocandin/LFAMB therapy with later step-down to fluconazole once stable and non-neutropenic; adjuvant corticosteroids may help prolonged disabling fever.
questions.beyond_mandell: Attribution of the transaminitis specifically to fluconazole hepatotoxicity and the post-HSCT differential (VOD, GVHD, viral hepatitis) rest on general HSCT/drug-toxicity knowledge, not this Mandell slice.

cohort_answer.text: A) Fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. DDX: hepatosplenic candidiasis (manifests at engraftment, median presentation 2-3 weeks post-HSCT if no ppx); CMV/VZV/EBV/HHV6/HSV/HBV (HSV highest risk pre-engraftment, usually on ppx); hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/VOD (elevated bili, hepatomegaly/RUQ pain, sudden weight gain, needs biopsy; risk factors liver dysfunction pre-tx, poorly matched donor, MTX for GVHD ppx); acute GVHD; other drugs (calcineurin inhibitor, methotrexate, TMP-SMX). B) CT abdomen/pelvis to work up hepatosplenic candidiasis; blood cultures for yeast; once cultures obtained, stop fluconazole, start echinocandin; if azole required use Posaconazole (reduced transaminitis); IDSA alternative: IV echinocandin or IV lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily; start empiric acyclovir for HSV if not on ppx; trend liver enzymes; look for non-infectious causes; consider esophageal brushings for yeast culture/sensitivity, Herpesviridae viral load.

questions.question: A cancer patient has fever with no obvious source clinically or radiographically. The patient is on piperacillin-tazobactam. The central venous line and peripheral lines are now growing a yeast-like organism.
questions.question_raw: Cancer patient with fever and no obvious source clinically or radiographically. On PipTazo. CVL and peripheral lines now growing a yeast-like organism.

parts.text: What is the source of the fever?
How would you investigate further?
Name 4 other potential sources of fever.
List 4 treatments for this situation.

parts_raw.text: What is the source of the fever?
How would you investigate further?

questions.model_answer:
a) Candidemia (invasive candidiasis), most likely catheter-associated (about 80% of candidemias occur in patients with a venous catheter as the likely source), though gut translocation across chemotherapy-damaged mucosa is an alternative source in this cancer patient.
b) (1) Repeat blood cultures from all lumens and a peripheral vein to confirm and follow clearance, with species identification (germ tube test/MALDI-TOF) and susceptibilities. (2) Dilated funduscopic ophthalmology examination in every candidemic patient to detect ocular candidiasis. (3) Echocardiography (transesophageal if persistently positive) for endocarditis, plus abdominal imaging if a deep source is suspected.
c) (1) Other bacterial infection/abscess. (2) Other fungal infection. (3) Viral infection. (4) Non-infectious causes such as the underlying malignancy, drug fever, or thrombosis.
d) (1) Start an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin) as first-line therapy. (2) Remove/replace the central venous catheter. (3) Step down to fluconazole once the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible, blood cultures have cleared, and the patient is stable. (4) Lipid-formulation amphotericin B as an alternative if intolerant/resistant. (Voriconazole is an option when added mold coverage is desired.)

cohort_answer.text: A) Fungemia - line associated or gut translocation (candidemia often from gut translocation rather than line, so don't always change lines if repeat culture negative). B) Repeat blood cultures from all lines; if Candida spp -> germ tube test; if Candida -> ophtho consult; abdominal imaging if source unclear; echocardiogram especially if persistently positive cultures. C) Infectious - bacterial (including abscess), viral, other fungal infection; Non-infectious - cancer, thrombosis, drug. D) Remove CVC; empiric echinocandin; stop PipTazo if not neutropenic; reduce immunosuppression if feasible. (IDSA alternatives: echinocandin, lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily, fluconazole 800mg loading then 400mg daily, voriconazole 400mg BID x2 doses then 200-300mg BID.)
